newsitem.title: USA: GCA June coffee stock data seen mainly neutral.
newsitem.headline: GCA June coffee stock data seen mainly neutral.

text.p: New York coffee futures are likely to be unimpressed by monthly inventory data released late Tuesday showing an increase in U.S. consumer coffee stocks, traders and analysts said.
Supplies of green coffee housed in U.S. warehouses rose in June by 139,000 60-kg bags, to 2,116,000 bags, the Green Coffee Association of New York reported.

Traders and analysts said the increase was mostly within expectations, with most estimates coming in at plus or minus 100,000 bags, although some market participants had predicted a build of up to 200,000 bags.
"It's more or less in line with expectations," said one trader. "I think it is already priced in the market. If it were 200,000 or above it would be viewed as bearish."
The port of New Orleans posted the largest gain in coffee stocks. New Orleans stocks rose by 64,000 bags to 917,000 bags, the GCA said.
Inventories increased by 44,000 bags, to 136,000 bags in Houston, Texas. Warehouse stocks in New York also increased in June, rising 42,000 bags to 331,000 bags.
In Laredo, Texas, however, inventories decreased by 65,000 bags, to 183,000 bags. Laredo is a major recieving point for coffee imported from Mexico.
Many analysts said the build up in stocks was to be expected with many producers selling coffee to take advantage of futures' surge to 20-year highs in late May.

"High prices dragged coffee out and I think the market will pretty much take it in stride," said Smith Barney analyst Walt Spilka. "I don't think this month is critical, but next month I expect stocks to go down."

Some traders, however, had expected a decline in consumer coffee inventories during June. They noted that in June 1996 stocks fell by 110,000 bags, to, to 2,161,000 bags. Typically, imports of coffee to the U.S. slow down during the summer ahead of the new-crop harvest of many Latin American countries, they said.
Although the GCA does not report the origin of the coffee stocks, some dealers suspected much of the coffee was robusta ot from Brazil -- beans not certifiable against the exchange.
"I think it was mostly Brazil and robustas," said Refco Inc. analyst Ann Prendergast. "What's wanted is higher quality Colombian milds and other milds."

While the monthly GCA data may not be particularly bearish by itself, combined with the recent increase in CSCE certified stocks and continued mild weather in top-grower Brazil, traders said futures' prices could come under pressure.

"I think the GCA was as expected, but I don't think there's any reason to buy this market," said Stephen Smith, the president of Miami-based South Futures. "There's no cold weather in Brazil, demand is curtailed during the summer, stockpiles have increased and the market settled badly on the charts."
CSCE benchmark September coffee closed down 4.15 cents per lb on Tuesday, to 157.85 cents, after ranging from 159.50 to 156.25. Spot July fell 2.50 cents, to 184.50 cents.
After the close on Tuesday, CSCE reported certified coffee stocks in the U.S. warehouses fell for the first time in more than a week, dipping 100 60-kg bags as of July 14, to 72,145 bags.
However, there were an additional 36,182 bags pending grading, the exchange said.
